messages.content: Write a post about what a software company learned from a year of remote work. Around 250 words.

**Twelve months, no office**

We gave up the lease in March. What follows is what actually shifted.

Meetings got worse first. In a room you can tell a conversation has ended, because people start gathering their laptops. On a call there's no such signal, so we spent 45 minutes on things worth 10. The fix was blunt: every recurring meeting dropped to 25 minutes, and any meeting nobody could write an agenda for got cancelled. That killed eleven out of nineteen.

Writing turned into the actual work. Our design docs used to be three bullets and a phone picture of a whiteboard. They run two pages now, and review comments moved from "lgtm" to things you can push back on. If everyone walked back into an office next week, that's the habit I'd fight to keep.

Onboarding fell apart. Before the move, a new hire shipped their first change in about four days. After, closer to three weeks. Nobody was overhearing anything anymore. What fixed it was assigning each newcomer a named buddy with an hour a day set aside, which costs real money and which worked.

Here's the part no one warned us about: people quit disagreeing. Disagreement needs somewhere cheap to happen, and Slack isn't cheap, because every objection sits there looking permanent and quotable. Our sharpest arguments used to happen while waiting for coffee. We never found a substitute. We tried three or four. All of them died.

Go back? No. But "remote is fine" is a smug answer. It's fine if you'll rebuild the parts of an office you never noticed you relied on.

---

**A year without an office**

We let the lease go in March. Here is what actually changed.

Meetings degraded immediately. In a room you can see a conversation end, because people close their laptops and shift in their chairs. A video call gives you none of that, so we burned 45 minutes on questions that deserved 10. Our answer was crude. Every recurring meeting was cut to 25 minutes, and any meeting without a written agenda got scrapped. Eleven of nineteen disappeared.

Then writing became the job. Our design docs had been three bullets and a blurry photo of a whiteboard. They run two pages now, and review comments went from "lgtm" to arguments you can answer. If we all filed back into an office tomorrow, that is the habit I would defend.

Onboarding broke. A new hire used to ship their first change in roughly four days. Afterward it took closer to three weeks, because nobody overheard anything anymore. The repair was a named buddy for every newcomer, one hour a day, reserved. It costs real money. It worked.

Nobody warned us about the last one: people stopped disagreeing. Disagreement needs a cheap place to happen, and Slack is expensive, since every objection sits there looking permanent and quotable. Our best arguments used to happen in line for coffee. We never replaced that. We tried three or four times. Each attempt died.

Would I go back? No. But "remote is fine" is a smug answer. It is fine if you are willing to rebuild the parts of an office you never noticed you were using.

---
